paras: The killing of Buck Beale was the death of a young Black man in a fight with a sheriff and a posse of fifteen citizens at his home ten miles west of Jefferson, Texas, on the night of Saturday, August 7, 1920. The posse had gone after Beale on an accusation that he had attacked a young white woman, a charge the dispatch stated as fact. An Associated Press brief carried the story to papers in Oklahoma, Arkansas and Texas, several of which headlined it as the killing of an attacker of a white woman.

According to the dispatch, Beale was accused of having attacked a young white woman shortly before the posse came for him. None of the versions names the woman, describes the alleged attack, or says whether a warrant had been issued.

On Saturday night the sheriff and a posse of fifteen citizens went to Beale's home ten miles west of Jefferson. The fullest version, printed in the Guthrie Daily Leader, said that Beale and others of his family barricaded the house and for a while stood off the posse, finally coming out with rifles. Beale was killed in the fight that followed. The reports do not name the sheriff or say who fired the fatal shot, and they do not say whether any family member or posse member was hurt.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any later investigation appears in the coverage, and no follow-up story was found.

The story circulated as a single short dispatch, dated August 9 in some papers and August 10 in others, and printed the victim's name as Beale, Beal or Beals. The Daily Ardmoreite and the Guthrie Daily Leader ran it on their front pages on August 10 under the heads "Negro attacks white woman and is killed by posse" and "Negro attacker of white woman, killed". The Morning Tulsa Daily World and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic used plainer headings, "Texas Negro Killed" and "Slain by Sheriff".

Five days later the Laredo Weekly Times reprinted the Associated Press item under the heading "Brute who attacked white woman killed in fight with Texas officers". Every version took the accusation and the posse's account of a fight as settled, and none gave a statement from Beale's family. No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Killing of Buck Beale
bases: Every report describes Beale as killed at his home in a fight with a sheriff and a posse of fifteen citizens after an accusation, with no custody or mob seizure reported (A1, A2, A5).

The only account, one wire dispatch, describes a sheriff-led posse of fifteen killing Beale in a gunfight at his barricaded home while pursuing him on an accusation of attacking a white woman, which is presented as lawful arrest action rather than a mob killing (A1, A2, A4). No other version, inquest or follow-up was found to test whether the killing exceeded lawful authority.
All five articles reprint one Associated Press dispatch from Jefferson with only small variants in wording and spelling, so no independent report confirms it (A1, A2, A5).

accounts.gist: Beale, after attacking a young white woman, was killed in a fight with the sheriff and a posse of fifteen at his home; in the fuller version he and his family barricaded the house, held off the posse, and finally came out with rifles.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'Negro attacker of white woman, killed' and 'Negro attacks white woman and is killed by posse' state the accusation as fact and present the killing as its consequence.
The Laredo Weekly Times headed the AP brief 'Brute who attacked white woman killed in fight with Texas officers'.
The Tulsa and Pine Bluff papers ran the dispatch under neutral heads, 'Texas Negro Killed' and 'Slain by Sheriff'.

conflicts.note: Variants of one wire text; Beale is the majority spelling.
Both place the killing on the preceding Saturday night; the date difference is in the dateline only.
